Evangelical Counsels
ee-van-JEL-ih-kul KOWN-sulz
n. pl. (in Roman theology, poverty, chastity and obedience: counsels held to be advised rather than commanded, and to constitute a higher state of perfection)
Greek euaggelion, gospel, through Latin evangelicus; with Latin consilium, counsel or advice, as distinguished from praeceptum, a precept.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

The evangelical counsels are poverty, chastity and obedience, classified in Roman theology as counsels rather than precepts: not commanded of all, but advised to those seeking perfection. The distinction between precept and counsel is the architecture of the whole two-tier system, and it is the point a Protestant must contest, because on it rests the claim that some Christians are more Christian than others. Scripture does not recognise the division. The law's demand is total and binds every man — “Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy mind” (Mat 22:37) leaves no residue of optional excellence to add. What Christ said to one rich young man he said to expose that man's idol, and Scripture draws the lesson about riches generally, not about a vocation for the few. Nor is perfection an attainment of a class: “Not as though I had already attained, either were already perfect: but I follow after” (Phi 3:12) is Paul, late in life, about himself. The counsels doctrine is therefore not a harmless taxonomy. It produces a church of two estates and a laity taught to expect less of itself than God requires of it.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines counsel as advice, opinion or instruction given upon request; precept as any commandment or order intended as an authoritative rule of action; and perfection as the state of being complete or without defect.

expand to see more

COUNSEL, n. Advice; opinion, or instruction, given upon request or otherwise, for directing the judgment or conduct of another.

PRECEPT, n. Any commandment or order intended as an authoritative rule of action; a mandate; a rule of moral conduct.

PERFECTION, n. The state of being perfect or complete, so that nothing requisite is wanting; also, a quality, endowment or acquirement completely excellent.

EVANGELICAL, a. According to the gospel; consonant to the doctrines of the gospel; sound in the doctrines of the gospel.

STATE, n. Condition; the circumstances of a being or thing at any given time; also, rank; condition; quality.

Key Scripture

Mat 22:37 — "Jesus said unto him, Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy mind."

Phi 3:12 — "Not as though I had already attained, either were already perfect: but I follow after, if that I may apprehend that for which also I am apprehended of Christ Jesus."

Luk 17:10 — "So likewise ye, when ye shall have done all those things which are commanded you, say, We are unprofitable servants: we have done that which was our duty to do."

Gal 3:10 — "For as many as are of the works of the law are under the curse: for it is written, Cursed is every one that continueth not in all things which are written in the book of the law to do them."

Modern Corruption

Poverty, chastity and obedience classed as advice rather than command: the doctrine that builds two tiers of Christian and lowers what is asked of the laity.

expand to see more

The corruption is the precept-and-counsel scheme itself. If the law is fully satisfied by precepts, a man may have works to spare, and from that surplus grow merit, supererogation and the treasury of the church. Christ closes the door: “when ye shall have done all those things which are commanded you, say, We are unprofitable servants: we have done that which was our duty to do” (Luk 17:10). There is no surplus. And the law's claim is not partial but entire: “Cursed is every one that continueth not in all things which are written in the book of the law to do them” (Gal 3:10).

The modern version of the same error is subtler and thrives in Protestant churches: a tier of the radical, the sold-out, the missionary, against whom the ordinary believer measures himself short. The principle to recover is that there is one standard, it is total, nobody meets it, and Christ has met it for his people. “with all thy heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy mind” (Mat 22:37) is addressed to everyone, and it leaves no room for a higher calling.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek euaggelion (G2098), gospel; Latin consilium, counsel; Greek entole (G1785), a commandment; Greek teleios (G5046), complete; Greek achreios (G888), unprofitable.

expand to see more

Latin consilium and praeceptum — counsel and command; the distinction the whole scheme rests on.

Greek entole (G1785) — a commandment; in Scripture every moral demand is one of these, never mere advice.

Greek teleios (G5046) — complete, whole, mature; “either were already perfect: but I follow after” (Phi 3:12).

Greek achreios (G888) — useless, unprofitable; “We are unprofitable servants” (Luk 17:10).

Greek euaggelion (G2098) — gospel; a word badly used in this phrase, since these counsels are law and not good news.

Usage

"“we have done that which was our duty to do” (Luk 17:10) — the sentence that abolishes a surplus of merit."

"“Not as though I had already attained” (Phi 3:12) — Paul declining the higher estate."

"“Cursed is every one that continueth not in all things” (Gal 3:10) — the law's totality, which leaves nothing optional."
